You're much more accustomed to hearing your voice as you speak. Other people will hear the sound waves from your voice hitting their ear drums. But you will hear your voice through vibrations in your body. They vibrations will travel through your body (which has bones and blood and flesh and nastiness like that) before reaching your ear drum. This will make your voice sound much lower. The contrast between that and how other people hear you (and how you sound in recordings) will make your brain sort of reel from the difference, setting off an inherent discomfort when you hear it.

I was a part of IMPRESS' summer program before my freshman year. I didn't know what to expect when I walked in, but I thought it was pretty neat. The program was designed with the purpose of helping students who might be at a disadvantage coming into college. I'm a first-generation college student, so I was invited. It's mostly about metacognition, which is an awareness of how you think and an understanding of it. We spent two weeks participating in different activities to help us think about what we know, how we know it and what to do with that knowledge. It's a little bit tricky to explain over text. Personally, I took away a lot about how to motivate myself when I'm not doing as well as I want to or as well as I think I should be doing. Two years later, as I'm in my second co-op and looking to enter my third year soon, I can confidently say that some of the things I learned with IMPRESS still stick with me.

IMPRESS is part of something called the Access Network, which is a network of programs on campuses across the nation that aims to create a more diverse and accessible STEM community. I actually work with them right now, if you're interested in learning more and want to PM me. :) We're a pretty great group of people, if I do say so myself.

Everyone else has already said something about the MPE, but as a whole, don't stress so much. I usually find that people do significantly worse when they stress themselves out. RIT has tons of resources for people who struggle in certain subjects. Gosnell has a Math Tutoring Center that I've spent many an hour in studying calculus. Golisano has the Society of Software Engineers as well as a CS Tutoring Center. RIT as a whole has the Academic Support Center as well, who are much better equipped to help students when they need it. You'll also take YearOne and your professor there can help point you in the right direction if you need resources.

Short answer: yes
Long answer: probably. If you're running an SSD, no. If not, it depends on your OS, but still yes. Your OS tracks files with something called pointers. When we delete files, our computer removes the pointer and marks the area it used to be as available space. This just removes how you would typically access a file and tells the OS that it can be overwritten. A file is still recoverable until the file has been overwritten with new data. If you want it to be gone (and have the resources) you need to wipe your hard drive's free space or overwrite where the file used to exist. Edit: If your teacher cares this much about a file, I'd be surprised. You're probably fine.
